question: Must I visit and serve a father who abused me as a child, or can I just make du'a for him?
asked: We always hear about the rights of the parents, over and over again. How about the rights of the children, and of those children who have been abused by their parents? My father was abusive, to the point that when I'm around him I get anxiety attacks and flashbacks and cannot breathe properly. I have moved on and live separately. Is it wajib for me to visit him and be a dutiful daughter, or can I just make du'a and let it be? What is my obligation? Do I have to serve him, given our past?
answer:
It is obvious that this sister has had a very traumatic childhood. And my answer to it is not therapy or counseling. It is not addressing the psychological issue; it is addressing the fiqh issue. I advise this sister, and anybody in that situation, that along with asking a shaykh and an Islamic person, also consult with a therapist and a counselor. Clearly, reading her email, she has a lot of trauma, as it's called, and she doesn't know how to unpack it.

And shaykhs are not therapists. Shaykhs are not counselors. We can give you the fiqh; we cannot give you therapy. And it is a mistake to come to any one of us who has Islamic knowledge with issues that require therapy, unless the person has trained in therapy. And I have not trained to be a counselor.

And we need to realize that abuse comes in many forms. In this particular case, it was physical and emotional. Physical abuse is, of course, hitting in a way that is obviously beyond what is normal. Now, what is normal varies from time to place to culture. When I grew up, it was much more common to hit. Before us, it was even more common to hit. And these days you can go to jail for doing the same thing that would have happened maybe in the 80s. But it is something that is cultural: how much is abuse and how much is discipline. And in our times, people are shying away from any type of hitting. Physical abuse means you do something that is traumatic physically.

There is emotional abuse. By the way, these are five types of abuse; you should know them. What is emotional abuse? Emotional abuse is you undermine the individual's sense of esteem, the individual's humanity: constantly criticizing, diminishing, name-calling. "Why were you born? You're a nuisance to me." Imagine if a parent says this. In this particular case, the sister mentions her father would always say, "I wish you had never been born." This is like, you haven't killed the daughter physically; you're killing her emotionally. What type of father would say this? What type of person would say this to a biological child of theirs, "I wish you had never been born"? Just imagine that level, right? Constantly, whatever criticism comes out, whatever it is that is being said: this is emotional abuse, where you're constantly diminishing. What's going to happen to a child being raised in that type of environment? How will they feel?

The third type of abuse is, of course, one of the worst types: sexual abuse, and we all know what that is.

And the fourth type of abuse is economic abuse. Economic abuse is that a person of means and wealth does not spend of that means and wealth on the family, and the family is not living a comfortable life even though the breadwinner has enough. Obviously, if he doesn't, then they're all suffering together. We're talking about a stingy person. And this is dhulm. All of these five types are dhulm. This is economic abuse.

And then the fifth is psychological abuse. Psychological abuse is similar to emotional, except that over here psychological abuse is fear and intimidation. It is a threatening that doesn't actually result in something physical, but a threat: "If you do this, I'm going to burn you. If you do this..." This is like psychological torture that is done to a person.

So these are five common types of abuse. And it must be said here: parents, adults, learn to recognize these types of abuse and monitor in your immediate families. If somebody is abusing a child within your own family, who is going to protect that child other than the extended family? Think about this. If you have somebody who is doing one of these types of abuse to a young person, it is our job collectively to come in. How else will this child be protected if it is being abused in its own house? And it is your cousin, your brother, your in-law, whatever. It must be our job to monitor collectively and then take the necessary steps.

And perhaps we might have an entire conference about this issue, because we need to teach the community how to recognize abuse and what to do in the case of abuse. And in fact, with some abuse, according to the law, if you are quiet, you will be prosecuted, according to the law of this country. And honestly, it's a good law. You cannot ignore some types of abuse when you see it in front of you and not do anything about it. We need to teach our community. So we need to be careful about recognizing these types of abuse.

And parents: the sister's email really shattered my heart. It really was traumatic to read. She went into detail; you already heard some. I'm not going to mention all of it, even though she said you can mention the detail, but I'd rather not go into it. The point is that, parents, we need to be cognizant that our children also have haqq over us. They have a haqq over us. And if we overstep that, if we cross the line, they can complain to Allah on Judgment Day that "my parents did zulm to me." Being a parent doesn't mean you get away with anything. Being a parent means it comes with responsibility.

And we see now, in the case of this daughter, that she is now an adult. She's left the household. She is saying that visiting her father makes her palpitate (what do you call it, the panic attack). Visiting brings back all of that. "I cannot even see him because of..." And she obviously has a detail of what is going on. And what is to be said in this case? What is the fiqh ruling over here? This young lady has now grown up, and her sense of self-worth, alhamdulillah, she's overcome to the point of starting a life, but now when she goes back, she feels diminished. She feels déjà vu all the way back.

So, response to her. Firstly, dear sister, before you get to the fiqh, please go see a therapist and counselor and unpack all of this trauma that you have. I cannot help you there. You need to go to an expert in this regard.

Secondly, when it comes to a fiqhi perspective, Allah subhanahu wa ta'ala mentions in the Qur'an: no soul is burdened with more than what it can bear. And if there are circumstances where you start suffering panic attacks or hyperventilating or palpitating, Allah is not calling you to do something that is unreasonable and beyond your bearing capability. And our Prophet ﷺ said, "La darar wa la dirar." This is a principle of fiqh: there shall be no harm inflicted, nor shall any harm be given. This is a general principle: no harming anybody.

So if she is being harmed psychologically, emotionally (and in this case her father was physically and emotionally abusive: physically, he would discipline too harshly, and emotionally, she has these phrases in her mind ringing all the time; this is abuse), and in this case, if she cannot overcome it, then **she is only obliged to do, of birr al-walidayn, what she is capable of doing.** So if she is financially stable and they need some money, she can send an amount indirectly; she doesn't have to go and hand it herself. The point is, there are still some duties, and the duties are diminished in light of the dhulm that has happened to her. To the extent that if it is such a harsh dhulm that she is frightened for her life, there are no duties upon her.

There are parents that physically harm their children. SubhanAllah, every once in a while we hear of a bizarre case where a parent, a'udhu billah, kills their child. This happens. It's human nature; in society it happens. It's against the fitrah, but we find this. Are you going to tell the child in that circumstance, "No, you still have to go"? No.

So listen to this rule: **the more the zulm increases, the less the huquq are there.** Simple as that. The more zulm has been done to you, the less you have to give back. And you have to make a judgment call in your own conscience, in front of Allah subhanahu wa ta'ala. And the shari'ah does not burden you with more than what you can bear. And that's why, as we know in the Qur'an:

> وَإِذَا الْمَوْءُودَةُ سُئِلَتْ ۝ بِأَيِّ ذَنبٍ قُتِلَتْ

Even that baby girl that is killed: the father does not have the right to just kill. This is zulm. And Allah will call the parents to task for zulm done to the children. So this is something both parties need to be aware of.

As for the sister, we say to her that Allah has tested you to raise your ranks; be patient. And also, also, please reach out to other family members and try to get some type of intervention and reconciliation. Have somebody from the family approach the father, or whoever is the perpetrator, because you never know. Maybe he might be repentant now and turn over a new leaf and ask for forgiveness, which is the ideal situation, in which case forgive for the sake of Allah and you will be forgiven.

Or maybe, maybe he doesn't realize the severity of what he's done, and he's in his own clueless world, and he doesn't understand now why the daughter is treating him so harshly, and he needs to be told, "No, you did these mistakes," or whatnot. Or maybe there is a perception issue, where she might have perceived something more than it was. All of these are possibilities.

She shouldn't just let it be. She should not be satisfied with the status quo. Don't just give up. Go through cousins, uncles, aunts, the mother if she's still on the same side or whatever, but try your best to see what can be done, and don't just be satisfied with the status quo. If it still doesn't work, and there is adamance or arrogance or whatnot, la yukallifullahu nafsan illa wus'aha, and you are not obliged to do more than what is necessary.

And the same goes for parents that have been missing. I've had a number of cases that come to me, and they say, for example, "My father completely abandoned us when I was born, and he completely walked out of our lives. Now when I'm 30, 35 years old, he has rediscovered us, and now he wants my money and whatnot." And the brother is like, "Why should I, after what he's done to my mother?" And obviously there's a lot of anger over there.

And the response is the same: as much zulm as was done to you, you have the right to diminish. But there's always some haqq, always some haqq, because at the end of the day it is your father or your mother. So you have to do what you can, what is reasonable to do. But there is no question that somebody who has done zulm does not have the same huquq as somebody who has been generous and kind. There is no question about this. La darar wa la dirar.

Then the final thing that needs to be said in all of these scenarios is: make du'a to Allah subhanahu wa ta'ala. Make du'a. Don't just let it go. Du'a solves everything. Our shari'ah teaches us that Allah is the one who brings hearts together. Allah is the one who is Muqallib al-Qulub. Allah is the one who says: if you tried every way to bring reconciliation, you couldn't have done it. If you spent the whole world's money, you couldn't have brought them together. Allah 'azza wa jall brought them together.

You do not know what will happen. So don't be satisfied with the status quo. Being satisfied with this status quo is not good; it might even be a sin. Try through your asbab, and then through Allah 'azza wa jall: make du'a to Allah to soften his heart, your heart. Try to mend ways in this dunya before the akhirah. And may Allah make it easy.

Final point for all of us here, parents and children: we both have an obligation to each other in this regard. And on Judgment Day, Allah tells us that parents and children will run away from each other. It's in the Qur'an, literally. Why will they run away from each other? Why will they run away? Because of these huquq. On the Day of Judgment, the father, the mother that has done zulm to their own son or daughter, when they see their son or daughter, they will run away, because they will know today is the day that huquq will be responded to.

So any parent who is mistreating, abusing a child, remember, that's what the Day of Judgment is for. And you and that child will be in front of the court of Allah 'azza wa jall, and everything will be plain. You don't want that day. Do not, do not do zulm to people who cannot defend themselves. The Prophet ﷺ warned us: the greatest zulm is against the du'afa, the people that cannot defend themselves. The greatest zulm that you can do is against those who cannot defend themselves. A child: mistreating a child, a'udhu billah, physically abusing, sexually.

And be monitoring this. This is one of those taboo topics we don't like to talk about, but it is a cancer in all of our society. It's not just our society; we know what happened in another faith tradition when it tried to hide what happened. We cannot do this. We have to address this head on. And that is why, maybe inshallah soon, maybe before or after Ramadan, we're going to have an entire seminar about abuse and recognizing abuse, understanding what constitutes abuse, learning what are techniques we can deal with, because we don't want this in our community, or in any community. We want to be communities of compassion and love. May Allah subhanahu wa ta'ala make all of our families families of love and compassion, and protect all of our children and women and all innocent ones.
